That is 90% below Haiku 4.5's $1.00 and $5.00. Cross 100,000 tokens and the rates become $0.50 and $2.50. That is a 50% cut, not a 90% cut. And Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku with an effort dial. The API default is medium. low, high, xhigh, and max are real settings. They change how much the model thinks, which changes the bill. entry.title: Why I Chose GDevelop Over Unity, Godot, and Construct (5 Reasons, 1 Dealbreaker)
entry.summary:
I ship one small 2D game to Google Play and web portals every month. I don’t do 3D and I don’t need fancy rendering. I need an engine that gets a finished game out the door without a fight. After months of testing, I put my time into GDevelop instead of Godot, Unity, or Construct 3. Here are the five reasons, the one thing it can’t do, and who should skip it.
1. Event sheets beat dense code I’m dyslexic, so walls of symbols and syntax are where I lose hours. In a text editor I’m hunting for a typo. In an event sheet I’m reading my game logic. I can work for hours without the mental fatigue.
2. Behaviors you drop on objects Drop the Platformer Object behavior on a sprite and you have a running, jumping character in about a minute. The behaviors are tested and compatible, so I skip the boilerplate and start on what makes the game mine. 3. Export that doesn’t eat my week
4. Everything lives in one place Less context switching means more flow state, and flow is what keeps a solo project moving. 5. Open source means nobody can reprice me The one thing GDevelop can’t do Takeaways Pick the tool that helps you finish games, not the one with the longest feature list Want to see this in action? I post a new GDevelop mechanic every few days: https://youtu.be/zwBISSibep4 Your turn: What engine are you using, and what’s the one thing that slows you down? Drop it in the comments. If you’re on the fence about GDevelop, ask me anything and I’ll answer. Follow me here for more solo dev workflows.

entry.title: The Confused Deputy Problem in AWS: ExternalId, aws:Source* Keys, and RCPs
entry.summary: Most IAM incidents people talk about start with a leaked access key or a wildcard that was too generous. The confused deputy problem is different. Nothing leaks. Every API call is authorized. CloudTrail shows a party you trust doing exactly what your policy lets it do. The only thing wrong is who asked it to. That is what makes it easy to miss in a review. This post covers the two variants AWS documents, cross-account and cross-service, the policy conditions that fix each one, and the details that decide whether the fix works in production. A confused deputy is a privileged party that gets talked into using its privileges for someone who doesn't have them.
